blocks.text: 3 January. The Brazilian side of Iguazu Falls

blocks.text:
After breakfast, you will visit the Brazilian side of the falls.

You can hear the water before reaching the main viewpoints, which offer a sweeping panorama of the entire system of cascades.

The name Iguazu is linked to the Guarani expression for ‘Big Water’. The route culminates at the Devil’s Throat, where an immense volume of water plunges into the canyon and thick spray fills the air.

The New Year period falls in the rainy season, so the torrents can be particularly powerful and wide.

**Iguazu Bird Park**

Optional.

**Price:** USD 50 per person.

**Macuco Safari at Iguazu Falls in Brazil**

**Price:** USD 130 per person.

A video recording of the trip can also be ordered separately.

blocks.text: 4 January. The Argentine side of Iguazu Falls and the Devil’s Throat

provenance.wordAbsenceReason: Word paragraph 78 dates the Argentine visit to January 5; no exact title matches the current assigned RU January 4 itinerary. Current RU dates are retained.

blocks.text:
Early in the morning, you will set off for the national park on the Argentine side of the falls.

The Ecological Train travels through the rainforest to the network of walking trails.

**Lower Circuit.** The paths cover about 1,700 metres and take approximately 1 hour 45 minutes. The route descends to the lower viewpoints of the Alvar Núñez, Elenita and Lanusse cascades. One of the most striking falls is Bosetti, which drops in an almost continuous wall of water.

**Upper Circuit.** This route is about 1,300 metres long and takes approximately 1 hour. The walkways pass above the torrents. Notable cascades include Adam and Eve.

**Devil’s Throat.** The path is about 1,000 metres long, with an estimated visit time of 1–1.5 hours. Water plunges 82 metres into a narrow cleft. The walkway leads almost to the edge, where the roar and spray become part of the experience.

After the tour, a transfer takes you back to the hotel.

On the Argentine side, the experience builds gradually. The lower route shows the cascades from below; the upper route lets you watch the water before it drops. The Devil’s Throat is the final stop, where water fills your field of vision and drowns out conversation. This is why several days are set aside for Iguazu: visits to the two sides offer different experiences.
